item.title: The 117-Year Lawsuit That May Have Inspired Dickens' 'Bleak House'
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth exploration of a historical legal case with cultural significance, providing a rich context for learning about literature and legal history.

The lawsuit at the center of Charles Dickensâs Bleak House, which ran in monthly installments from 1852 to 1853, is a family dispute over a will that has been in the Court of Chancery for so long that âno man alive knows what it means.â When Jarndyce and Jarndyce is finally wound up, the estate it was fought over is gone: it has been âabsorbed in costs,â as the novel puts it. So which real case was Dickens poking at?

The answer youâll hear most often comes with a doozy of a number attached, a suit filed in 1798 that supposedly dragged on until 1915.

Two Suits, No Names

Dickens kicked off the guessing game himself in the preface he wrote in August 1853, the same one where he defended the spontaneous combustion of Krook: he insisted that âeverything set forth in these pages concerning the Court of Chancery is substantially true, and within the truth,â and then pointed to two real cases without naming either one. The first had been going for nearly 20 years and had cost Â£70,000, and was, he wrote, âA FRIENDLY SUIT.â The second, still undecided, âwas commenced before the close of the last century and in which more than double the amount of seventy thousand pounds has been swallowed up in costs.â

The first is usually identified as the fight over the will of Charles Day, a rich manufacturer of boot blacking, which is a nice irony for a man who spent part of his childhood pasting labels on blacking pots. The second, according to legal historian Patrick Polden, was the Jennens case.

William the Rich

William Jennens died at his country house in Acton, Suffolk, in June 1798, in his late 90s. The Monthly Magazine called him the supposed richest commoner in England. The Gentlemanâs Magazine said his property was thought to be worth at least Â£2 million, that dividends on most of his stocks hadnât been collected since 1788, and that an iron chest held Â£19,000 in banknotes from that year. It also reported a will found in his coat pocket, sealed but never signed: according to his favorite servant, Jennens had left his spectacles at home on the day he went to his lawyer to sign it, and then forgot about it.

So the estate went to his relatives under the law, and for more than a century people named Jennens or Jennings, in Britain and in the U.S., tried to prove they were the ones who should have gotten it. In January 1915, American papers ran an Associated Press item about the death of David Jennings in the Wolverhampton workhouse, âfamous in legal circlesâ as a claimant to the âJenningsâ Millions,â which the item said Dickens had used as the basis for Jarndyce and Jarndyce. That may be where the 1915 end date comes from, though one version of the story noted that the case hadnât been reopened in about 40 years.

The Case Against the Case

The 117-year version says the case ended when legal fees had eaten the whole estate, just like in the book. Polden, who went through the court records for a two-part study in the Common Law World Review, says that isnât what happened. Jennensâs property was handed out to his next of kin, and the lawsuits that followed were separate claims by would-be heirs, who lost every significant ruling but one. In Jennens, he writes, âthere was no such fund, no ongoing case and the deadly refrain of âcosts in the causeâ did not echo down the years.â The litigation had been dormant for 15 years by the time Dickens started writing Bleak House in November 1851, and Polden calls the idea that Dickens fictionalized it âseriously misleading.â

Polden does allow that Dickens may have been thrown by a strange news episode in 1852, when papers announced the case had been settled and then took it back. And there were other candidates all along. The will of Peter Thellusson, who died in 1797, was fought over in court until the House of Lords upheld it in 1806, and a new dispute over the fortune broke out in 1858. The only link Polden found that really ties the Jennens case to the novel is a backward one: once Bleak House started coming out, people said the real case resembled the fictional one.

item.title: Every Stanley Kubrick Movie, Ranked by Rotten Tomatoes
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engages with a significant filmmaker's work, offering a nuanced ranking that can be informative and thought-provoking for an English learner interested in film

Perhaps the singular genius of director Stanley Kubrick was his ability to handle multiple genres with equal aplomb. Every Kubrick movie is visually stylish, with nuanced storytelling and imaginative framing. Arguably, there's no such thing as a bad Kubrick film, but this overview, ranked according to Rotten Tomatoes critics, will prompt some fascinating debates between cinephiles.

1. Dr. Strangelove Or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb (1964) // 97%

Sitting in top spot with a remarkable 97% rating is Kubrick's 1964 classic cold war satire, which stars Peter Sellers. Sterling Hayden plays Brigadier General Jack D. Ripper, the unhinged officer one button-press away from ordering an unwarranted nuclear strike. Sellers is unforgettable as a trio of charactersâBritish RAF officer Lionel Mandrake, the President of the United States, and the titular âexpert,â Dr. Strangelove.

2. Paths of Glory (1957) // 96%

Kubrick was ahead of his time with this nuanced World War I movie which follows officer Colonel Dax (Kirk Douglas) and his French soldiers, tasked with carrying out a suicidal attack on a fortified German position. Itâs a humane and deeply moving film based on the Humphrey Cobb novel of the same name.

3. The Killing (1956) // 96%

This transcendent neo noir thriller stars Sterling Hayden as criminal Johnny Clay, who recruits a diverse team including a bartender, a betting teller, a corrupt cop, and a sharpshooter, to rob millions from a racetrack. When the teller (Elisha Cook Jr.) lets slip the plan to his wife, things swiftly go awry.

4. 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) // 91%

Seven decades on, Kubrick's visionary sci-fi movie still stands as one of the all-time best of the genre. Highly influential for its striking visual style and meditative nature, the director masterfully co-wrote this tale with another acknowledged great, sci-fi writer and inventor Arthur C. Clarke.

5. Spartacus (1960) // 90%

This fantastic sword and sandals epic follows Spartacus the slave's journey from trainee gladiator to rebel leader. With Kirk Douglas as the eponymous hero, and a terrific supporting cast of Laurence Olivier, Jean Simmons, and Tony Curtis, this movie delivers on every level.

6. Full Metal Jacket (1987) // 84%

One of the best cinematic takes on the Vietnam War, Full Metal Jacket is as memorable for its brutal training camp scenes as its portrayal of American soldier's experiences on the battlefield. R. Lee. Ermey steals the show as a threatening drill sergeant, with Matthew Modine starring as Private James T. âJokerâ Davis.Â The movie was adapted from Gustav Hasfordâs semi-autobiographical novel The Short-Timers.

7. A Clockwork Orange (1971) // 83%

Not for the faint of heart, this eerie crime drama, based on the book by Anthony Burgess, follows young hoodlum and his cold-hearted gang of âdroogs'âas they rampage through a truly disturbing version of England. Malcolm McDowellâs portrayal of Alex is a thing of wonder.

8. Lolita (1962) // 83%

As controversial as it is misunderstood, Kubrick adapted Vladimir Nabokovâs story of an older man's obsession with an underage girl with insight and bravery. James Mason is unforgettable as the tortured, black-souled Humbert Humbert, with Sue Lyon putting in a remarkable performance as the titular character, and Shelley Winters as her naive mother.

9. Killerâs Kiss (1955) // 81%

Aging boxer Davey Gordon (Jamie Smith) travels into the city's underbelly to rescue his dancer girlfriend Gloria (Irene Kane) from the clutches of her nefarious boss. Frank Silvera is suitably menacing as the baddie in this lean, stylish thriller.

10. Eyes Wide Shut (1999) // 79%

A beautiful, at times surreal and hallucinogenic, exploration of lust and fidelity, Eyes Wide Shut stars Tom Cruise and Nicole Kidman. It follows the former's descent into an elite and disturbing sexual society while navigating his own marriage.

11. Barry Lyndon (1975) // 77%

William Makepeace Thackeray's classic novel about an 18th century Irishman's ruthless climb to the heights of English nobility is transformed by Kubrick into a optically sumptuous affair, with Ryan O'Neal a commanding presence as Lyndon.

12. The Shining (1980) // 75%

Kubrick's sole foray into the horror genre was truly groundbreaking. Based on the novel by Stephen King, The Shining stands as one of the best of its kind, with Jack Nicholson starring as a struggling writer who makes the unwise decision to take a job as caretaker of an isolated hotel.

13. Fear and Desire (1953) // 70%

In last place with a respectable 70% rating is Kubrick's debut, an intriguing study of the madness of war. Trapped behind enemy lines during a conflict between two unspecified countries, four soldiers face madness and mortality as they seek to return home.

item.title: The Wealthiest Person in Every State, Mapped
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: While informative, the article leans towards listicle format and may not provide the depth of learning or the quality of writing expected by the advanced Englis

There's at least one person in every state whose wealth eclipses everyone else, but who is that person in your state?

Forbes took a look at the wealthiest person in each state to figure out which industry you have to be in if you want to be the wealthiest, and which states top the list for the riches of the rich. Some states may surprise you with someone you never heard of, while others may not shock you with who tops the list.

So where do the richest of the rich rank in each state? Here are a few things to know about the wealthiest people in different states.

Tech Gives a Big Boost

Several states can brag that their wealthiest resident came from the tech industry. In fact, the top five states with the richest residents all come from the tech sector.

Texas leads the pack with the richest person in the world calling the Lone Star State their home state. Elon Musk is estimated to be worth $1 trillionâyes, that's trillion with a T. The tech CEO owns Tesla and SpaceX, with the latter offering an IPO in June 2026 that pushed his net worth above the $1 trillion mark.

Second-place Florida is home to Jeff Bezos, the founder of Amazon, who lives in the Sunshine State along with his estimated worth of $381 billion. One advantage for billionaires like Bezos living in the state is its lack of an individual income tax on that money.

Sergey Brin is the co-founder of Google, starting the company in 1998 along with Larry Page. Today, that company is worth a lot of money, which has made him rich. Brin is worth an estimated $265 billion and calls Nevada his main residenceâhome to Lake Tahoe and Brin's home on its shores, which alone costs more than $40 million.

It may be a surprise, then, to see all these tech executives leading the list for being the wealthiest people in the state they live in and not seeing California higher on that list. The state ended up in fourth place, with billionaire Mark Zuckerberg pushing the state into the top five states with the richest resident. The Facebook leader is worth $246 billion, making him the richest Californian. That's quite a feat in the state with the most billionaires, with Zuckerberg only one of almost 200 billionaires in California.

Steve Ballmer rounds out the top five as Washingtonâs richest resident. Companies like Starbucks, Amazon, and Costco call the state home, but it's Ballmer's work at Microsoft that put him at the top of the list of richest residents. He was the company's CEO from 2000 to 2014.

Not Just Tech at the Top

While each state has a richest resident, you may be surprised at how much some are worth.

Nebraska, for example, ranks sixth for its richest resident. Warren Buffett, nicknamed the Oracle of Omaha, is worth $147 billion from his investments in his company Berkshire Hathaway.

The only other person on the list worth more than $100 billion is Rob Walton, the richest resident in Arkansas. He earned his fortune from his connection to the retailer Walmart. His father, Sam Walton, founded the company.
